scenes.label: Introduction
beats: Every day, we share information through websites, mobile applications, banking systems and cloud platforms.
But have you ever wondered what actually keeps this information secure?
Cybersecurity is built around three fundamental principles. Together, they form the CIA Triad.
Confidentiality. Integrity. Availability.

scenes.label: Understanding the Triad
beats: Let us look at the three principles, one by one.
Confidentiality protects information from unauthorised access. It answers one simple question. Who is allowed to see this?
Integrity protects information from unauthorised change. It asks, is this data accurate, complete and trustworthy?
Availability ensures that information and services remain accessible whenever authorised users need them.
Effective security requires all three. A system that is private but always offline, or available but easily altered, is not secure.

scenes.label: Confidentiality
beats: Consider an online banking application. Anyone on the internet can open the login page. But only the account holder should ever see the account.
It begins with authentication. Proving who you are, using your customer ID and password, and often a second factor, such as a one-time code.
Authentication is followed by authorisation, which decides what an identified user is permitted to do.
Access control enforces those permissions. A customer may view their own account, but never the account of another customer.
Data is also protected while it travels. Encryption converts readable information into ciphertext, which only the intended receiver can decrypt.
Here is a familiar example. A student logs in to the examination portal and views their own results. Another student's record is refused, because they are not authorised to see it.
In short, confidentiality is about preventing unauthorised access to information.

scenes.label: Integrity
beats: Integrity is about accuracy. Information must remain exactly as it was recorded, unless it is changed by someone who is authorised to change it.
Imagine a transfer of one thousand rupees. The amount is stored in a database, and sent to another system for processing.
Now suppose an attacker intercepts the transfer and changes the amount to ten thousand rupees. The record still looks valid. But it is no longer true.
Cryptographic hashing prevents this. A hash function converts data into a short, fixed-length fingerprint. Change even one character, and the fingerprint changes completely.
Digital signatures go further. They prove who created or approved the data, and confirm that it has not been altered since.
File integrity checks compare hashes before and after transfer, and audit logs record every change, along with who made it, and when.
For example, a published university result must not be secretly modified. Integrity is about maintaining data accuracy and trustworthiness.

scenes.label: Availability
beats: Availability ensures that information and services are accessible to authorised users, whenever they are needed.
A student opens the university website to download their results. The page loads normally, and the service is healthy.
Now imagine a sudden flood of requests, far beyond what the server can handle. Response times rise, queues fill up, and eventually the service fails. This is a denial of service attack.
Availability is engineered in advance. A load balancer spreads traffic across several servers, so that no single machine carries the entire load.
Servers are duplicated, so if one fails, another takes over. Backups protect the data itself, and disaster recovery plans restore service after a major failure.
With these controls in place, the service recovers, and the student can download the result again.
Availability means access to information when it is needed, not merely when everything happens to be working.

scenes.label: Working Together
beats: In practice, the three principles are never separate. They work together, in the same system, at the same moment.
Think about a single banking transaction. Confidentiality ensures that only you, the authenticated customer, can see your account and your balance.
Integrity ensures that the amount you entered is the amount that is recorded and transferred, unchanged.
Availability ensures that the application, the database, and the payment network are reachable at the moment you press confirm.
Remove any one of them, and the system is no longer trustworthy. A private but tampered balance is useless. An accurate balance that nobody can reach is equally useless.
Complete information security means protecting all three, together.

scenes.label: Real-World Applications
beats: These principles appear in every industry that holds sensitive information.
In banking, confidentiality protects account details, integrity protects the transaction ledger, and availability keeps payments running around the clock.
In healthcare, confidentiality protects patient records, integrity protects prescriptions and test results, and availability gives doctors access during an emergency.
In education, confidentiality protects student data, integrity protects marks and certificates, and availability keeps examination and admission portals open on result day.
The technology differs. The principles do not.

scenes.label: Recap
beats: So, when you evaluate any system, ask three questions. Confidentiality. Who can access the information?
Integrity. Is the information accurate and trustworthy?
Availability. Can authorised users access it when needed?

The next time you use an application, access a website, or share information online, remember that these three principles are working behind the scenes. Confidentiality, integrity and availability are not just cybersecurity terminology. They are the foundation of digital trust.
